harbor.practice: Harbor's 4.2M documents become ≈ 38M chunks; at 768 dims in int8 that is ≈ 29 GB of vectors per replica before graph links and metadata.
harbor.failure: Treating raw vector bytes as total storage or RAM demand.
harbor.tryIt: In the calculator, enter Harbor's 4.2 million documents and adjust pages and tokens until you get about 38 million chunks. Then read the RAM with int8 vectors, 2 replicas and graph links.

store.fitNote: listings plus reviews, re-embedded on every model change
store.practice: {company} indexes about 2 million listings plus their reviews. Listings are short, one chunk each, but reviews multiply the count into tens of millions of vectors, so the embedding bill for a model change became a line in the migration plan.
store.failure: Sizing from listings alone and forgetting reviews, Q&A and size charts.
store.tryIt: In the calculator, set 2 million documents, 1 page of 300 tokens, 256-token chunks, 768 dimensions, int8 and 3 replicas. Then add 20 million reviews of about 80 tokens as separate documents and compare.

bank.fitNote: retention, not today's volume, drives size
bank.practice: {company}'s policy corpus is small; its large collection is dispute case notes, retained for years, so growth and retention drive sizing more than today's size.
bank.failure: Sizing for today's case volume without the multi-year retention period.
bank.tryIt: Estimate the vectors for 400 cases a day kept for 7 years at 2 chunks each (about 2 million), then enter that into the calculator as documents.

travel.fitNote: hotel content in several languages dominates
travel.practice: {company} indexes fare rules (small) and hotel content (hundreds of thousands of properties with descriptions and reviews in several languages); hotel content dominates storage.
travel.failure: Forgetting that each language version of a hotel description is a separate set of chunks.
travel.tryIt: In the calculator, model 300,000 hotels × 2 languages × 1 page of 400 tokens, and compare float32 with int8.

harbor.practice: A Harbor parser pod crashed after writing chunks but before acking; redelivery produced no duplicates because chunk IDs are deterministic and writes carry a version guard.
harbor.failure: Watching worker latency while the queue's oldest-message age grows: that is a freshness incident.
harbor.fitNote: deterministic chunk IDs made redelivery harmless
harbor.tryIt: In the ingestion simulation, set arrivals above worker capacity with backpressure off, then on, and watch queue length and lag. Then write Harbor's chunk-ID formula (document ID + version + position).

store.fitNote: price and stock changes arrive in bursts
store.practice: Sellers update prices and stock in bursts, especially before a sale. {company}'s ingestion pulls from a queue with backpressure, writes with a version guard so an old price never overwrites a new one, and sends unparseable seller uploads to a dead-letter queue.
store.failure: Acknowledging the queue message before the index write commits, so a crash loses the price update.
store.tryIt: In the simulation, set a 5% poison rate and watch the dead-letter queue. Then write the compare-and-set rule for a price update: write only if the incoming version is newer than the stored one.

bank.fitNote: notes that fail PII scrubbing are never indexed
bank.practice: {company}'s case-notes pipeline is idempotent (chunk IDs from case ID, note version and position), and every write carries a version guard. A dead-letter queue holds notes that fail PII scrubbing, for human review, instead of indexing them.
bank.failure: Indexing a note that failed PII scrubbing because the pipeline treats scrubbing errors as warnings.
bank.tryIt: Write the ingestion steps for rows of disputes.csv as queue messages, including a dead-letter path for any text your scrubber cannot process.

travel.fitNote: supplier feeds arrive late and out of order
travel.practice: Supplier fare-rule feeds arrive late and out of order. {company} applies each with a version guard, so yesterday's rule never overwrites today's.
travel.failure: Applying supplier updates in arrival order instead of by version.
travel.tryIt: Write three out-of-order update events for one fare rule and show which writes the version guard accepts.

harbor.practice: Harbor's travel policy table (rows = regions, columns = per-day limits) is stored as structured rows; flattening it had caused wrong per-diem answers.
harbor.failure: Assuming a parse that produced lots of text was read correctly.
harbor.fitNote: a flattened per-diem table gave wrong answers
harbor.tryIt: Take a table-heavy PDF of your own, extract it with pdfplumber or Docling, and compare a flattened text line with row-as-sentence chunks; then ask a local model a per-cell question with each.

store.fitNote: size charts arrive as images and PDFs
store.practice: Seller size charts arrive as images and PDFs. {company} OCRs them, extracts the table to rows, and stores row-as-sentence chunks such as “Size M: chest 40 in, length 28 in”.
store.failure: Flattening a size chart into one line, so the assistant reports the wrong measurement for a size.
store.tryIt: Write a size chart as a small table, flatten it to one line and to row-as-sentence chunks, and ask a local model “What is the chest size for L?” with each.

bank.practice: {company} receives scanned dispute forms, bank statements and cheques. OCR confidence is recorded per page, low-confidence pages go to human review, and statement tables are stored as structured rows.
bank.failure: Assuming a statement parse with lots of text is correct when columns of amounts were merged.
bank.tryIt: Create a two-column statement table (date, amount) in a document, export it to PDF, extract it with pdfplumber, and check whether every amount stays with its date.

travel.practice: Hotel policies arrive as PDFs with tables of cancellation charges by date range. {company} extracts each row as a sentence with the hotel ID, so “cancel 3 days before” finds the right charge.
travel.failure: Indexing a cancellation-charge table as flat text, so the date ranges and percentages come apart.
travel.tryIt: Write a three-row cancellation table, extract it as rows, and test a question about the middle date range.

harbor.practice: Harbor's freshness SLO is "99% of edits searchable within 10 minutes; deletions within 5", measured per change from source timestamp to index timestamp.
harbor.failure: Deleting the source file and forgetting the vectors, caches and summaries derived from it.
harbor.tryIt: Write the lineage record for one chunk of a policy in policies.json, then list what must be rebuilt if the parser version changes.

store.fitNote: removed listings and changed prices must vanish quickly
store.practice: When a listing is removed or its price changes, {company} replaces its chunks atomically and purges cached answers that cite it. The freshness target is 99% of price changes searchable within 2 minutes.
store.failure: Removing the listing but leaving its cached answers, so {assistant} keeps recommending a product that is no longer sold.
store.tryIt: For a product in products.csv, write the events for a price change and for a deletion, and list every store (index, caches, summaries) each must update.

bank.fitNote: deletion requests reach vectors and summaries too
bank.practice: When a customer exercises a deletion right, {company} removes their case notes from the index, caches and any derived summaries within the legal deadline, and keeps lineage to prove it.
bank.failure: Deleting the source notes but not the vectors and summaries derived from them.
bank.tryIt: Write a reconciliation job in pseudo-code that lists the case IDs in disputes.csv, compares them with an index's IDs, and reports what to delete.

travel.practice: Fare rules change with supplier contracts. {company} tracks indexed_at − source_modified_at for every rule and alerts when the p99 exceeds 15 minutes.
travel.failure: Measuring freshness for edits but not for deletions of withdrawn fares.
travel.tryIt: Invent source and index timestamps for ten rule updates, compute each lag, and report the p90.

harbor.practice: Harbor's three largest customers have dedicated shards; the other 1,197 share placement-by-hash shards, and a tenant is promoted when it passes 5M chunks or 50 QPS.
harbor.failure: Adding replicas to fix an ingestion bottleneck; replicas help reads, not writes.
harbor.fitNote: dedicated shards for the largest customers
harbor.tryIt: In the shard figure, set the largest tenant to 40% of traffic and compare the three placements. Then write Harbor's promotion rule (over 5M chunks or 50 QPS) as code.

store.fitNote: large sellers and sale-week read peaks
store.practice: {company} partitions listings by category and hash, not by seller, because a few large sellers would otherwise overload their shards. Before sales, read replicas are added ahead of the traffic peak.
store.failure: Adding replicas to speed up a backfill. Replicas help reads, not writes.
store.tryIt: In the figure, raise the largest tenant to 70% and see which placement survives. Then decide how {company} should place its ten largest sellers.

bank.practice: {company} is a single tenant with a modest index; sharding matters only for its case-notes archive.
bank.failure: Designing multi-tenant sharding for a single-tenant system.
bank.tryIt: Use the figure to explain to a colleague why hash placement makes every query fan out to every shard.

travel.practice: {company}'s hot spot is not a tenant but a season: monsoon and holiday weeks multiply queries for a few destinations.
travel.failure: Planning replicas from average traffic instead of peak-season destinations.
travel.tryIt: In the figure, treat the largest tenant as a peak-season destination at 50% of traffic and compare the placements.

harbor.practice: When an employee leaves Finance, Harbor's deny list blocks Finance documents for them immediately, before the next ACL sync updates the index.
harbor.failure: Filtering restricted documents after the model has already seen them.
harbor.fitNote: a deny list blocks revoked access before the next sync
harbor.tryIt: In the revocation figure, set a 30-minute sync with no deny list and count the red dots; then turn on the deny list and the scope-keyed cache and count again.

store.fitNote: sellers see only their own orders and payouts
store.practice: {company}'s permission problem is sellers: a seller-dashboard assistant must see only that seller's orders, payouts and messages, enforced by a server-set seller ID filter on every query.
store.failure: Taking the seller ID from the chat (“I am seller 1042”) instead of the authenticated session.
store.tryIt: Write the retrieval filter for a seller-assistant query, plus three cross-seller probe questions that must return nothing.

bank.practice: {company}'s staff assistant filters case notes by the agent's team and case assignment. When an agent is moved off a case, a deny list blocks it immediately, and cached answers are keyed by access scope.
bank.failure: Relying on the instruction “do not reveal other customers' data” instead of filtering before retrieval.
bank.tryIt: In the revocation figure, model an agent removed from a case at minute 5 and find the settings that give zero red dots.

travel.fitNote: partner agencies see only their own bookings
travel.practice: Partner agencies use {assistant} too. Each agency sees only its own bookings, enforced by a server-set agency ID, with separate collections for the largest partners.
travel.failure: Caching a booking answer without the agency in the cache key, so another agency receives it.
travel.tryIt: Write the cache key for “show my upcoming bookings”, including user, agency and policy version, and explain each field.

harbor.practice: Harbor's index manifest binds embedder v2 to index v2; rollback switches both the alias and the query encoder together.
harbor.failure: Assuming equal vector dimensions make two embedding models compatible.
harbor.fitNote: the manifest binds the embedder to the index
harbor.tryIt: In the blue/green figure, try to cut over before the backfill, then follow the steps in order; note which guard stopped each premature step.

store.fitNote: re-embedding tens of millions of vectors needs a plan
store.practice: Moving to a multilingual embedding model meant re-embedding {company}'s tens of millions of listing and review vectors. It ran blue/green with dual writes during the backfill, an offline benchmark per language and a 5% canary before the alias switch.
store.failure: Switching the query encoder before the new index finished backfilling, so half the catalogue was invisible.
store.tryIt: Run the figure in order, then write {company}'s migration checklist with a cost estimate from the 10.1 calculator.

bank.fitNote: a warm old index keeps rollback an alias change
bank.practice: {company} versions its policy index with a manifest (embedder, chunker, parser) and keeps the old index warm for two weeks after a switch, so a rollback is an alias change.
bank.failure: Retiring the old index on cut-over day, which leaves no rollback.
bank.tryIt: Write the manifest fields for {company}'s policy index and a three-step rollback runbook.

travel.fitNote: a chunker change is a migration too
travel.practice: Changing the chunker for fare rules is also a migration: {company} built v4 from stored text, compared retrieval on its rule questions, then switched the alias.
travel.failure: Treating a chunker change as a small config tweak and editing the live index in place.
travel.tryIt: In the figure, roll back after the canary step and explain why the rollback window matters.

harbor.practice: Harbor's benchmark replays 2,000 logged queries with real ACL filters while 5% of the corpus is updated, and reports p95 latency and Recall@10 together.
harbor.failure: Benchmarking with repeated identical queries, which mostly measures the cache.
harbor.fitNote: logged queries replayed with real ACL filters during updates
harbor.tryIt: Run the laptop ANN benchmark at 100,000 vectors, then 1 million if your RAM allows, and record recall against efSearch. List what it does not test: filters, writes, real embeddings.

store.fitNote: festival load with price updates streaming in
store.practice: {company} benchmarks search by replaying logged shopper queries with stock and pincode filters while price updates stream in at festival rates, and reports p95 latency and Recall@10 together.
store.failure: Benchmarking without filters. A pincode filter that leaves 2% of listings changes ANN behaviour completely.
store.tryIt: Write the benchmark plan: query sample, filter selectivity, update rate, target QPS, metrics and three scale steps.

bank.practice: {company}'s corpus is small, so its benchmark focuses on latency under concurrent case-note writes and on labelled retrieval quality, not on ANN tuning.
bank.failure: Copying a vendor's million-vector benchmark that has nothing in common with a small, filtered, write-heavy workload.
bank.tryIt: Time exact search over embedded policy texts while a loop inserts 1,000 new vectors, and report the p95 latency.

travel.fitNote: hotel search with destination and date filters at peak
travel.practice: Hotel search is benchmarked with real destination and date filters while replaying peak-season traffic.
travel.failure: Benchmarking with repeated identical queries, which mostly measures the cache.
travel.tryIt: Write a hotel-search query sample that varies destination, dates and language, and explain why repeated queries would mislead.

harbor.practice: Only 6% of Harbor queries were multi-hop; query decomposition fixed most of them, so a knowledge graph was deferred.
harbor.failure: Adopting an advanced retrieval technique because of its name, without a failure analysis showing the gap.
harbor.fitNote: a knowledge graph deferred after failure analysis
harbor.tryIt: Classify 20 of your own policy questions as single-hop, multi-hop or document-level, and decide which advanced technique, if any, the counts justify.

store.practice: {company} evaluated late interaction for queries with many exact attributes (“M, 100% cotton, round neck”). It helped only on that slice, so it runs as a reranker for attribute-heavy queries rather than for all search.
store.failure: Adopting GraphRAG for product search because it is fashionable, without a failure analysis.
store.tryIt: Watch the MaxSim animation, then compute MaxSim by hand for a 3-token query against two product titles, using similarities you assign.

bank.fitNote: aggregate questions belong to SQL, not retrieval
bank.practice: Some {company} questions are aggregates (“which merchants had the most disputes this month?”). Those go to SQL over structured data, not to vector search or a knowledge graph.
bank.failure: Answering aggregate questions by retrieving a few chunks and letting the model count.
bank.tryIt: Answer “which merchant category has the most fraud?” from transactions.csv with pandas, then explain why retrieving a few chunks would get it wrong.

travel.fitNote: agentic retrieval across fares, hotels and disruptions
travel.practice: {assistant} routes between sources (fare rules, hotel content, live disruptions) with a small agentic retriever, because one pipeline cannot serve such different sources.
travel.failure: Letting the agent call every source for every question, multiplying latency and cost.
travel.tryIt: Write routing rules for five traveller questions: which source each needs, and in what order.

harbor.scenario: Generate the 1,000 documents from templates based on policies.json, with tenants and access_groups. The revocation test removes a user from the leadership group and proves the salary-band and reorganisation documents never reach their context.

store.scenario: Generate 1,000 listings from products.csv templates. Inject a burst of price updates delivered out of order, a deleted listing whose cached answer must also disappear, and one seller with ten times the traffic of the others.

bank.scenario: Generate 1,000 case notes from disputes.csv. Inject notes that fail PII scrubbing (they must reach the dead-letter queue, not the index), a deletion request for one customer, and an agent moved off a case (revocation).

travel.scenario: Generate fare-rule and hotel documents from fare_rules.json templates. Inject supplier updates that arrive out of order, a withdrawn fare that must disappear, and a chunker change that becomes a blue/green migration.
